title: Why Is a Rainbow Always at the Same Angle?

beats: A rainbow looks like it's painted on the sky.
But try walking toward one, and it backs away.
Move to the side, and it moves with you.
That's because a rainbow isn't a thing in the sky. It's an angle.
And that angle is always the same: forty-two degrees. Here's why.
Start with a single raindrop, and a single ray of sunlight.
A small raindrop is not shaped like a teardrop. It's very nearly a perfect sphere, and that matters, because a sphere treats every ray by the same rule.
When the ray hits the surface, it goes in, and it bends, because light travels more slowly in water than in air.
It crosses the drop, and at the back surface, part of it reflects.
Then it crosses the drop again and leaves through the front, bending a second time.
So the drop sends that light back toward the side the sun is on.
How far the light gets turned depends on where it hits the drop.
A ray through the dead centre bounces straight back.
Move the ray up a little, and it comes back at a small angle.
Move it higher, and the angle grows.
But watch what happens near the top.
The angle stops growing. It reaches a maximum of about forty-two degrees, and then it starts to shrink again.
That turning point is the whole secret.
Look at the curve. On the steep part, a small change in where the ray enters makes a big change in where it leaves, so that light gets smeared across many angles.
But at the top, the curve is flat. There, a whole band of rays shares almost the same direction.
Sunlight doesn't hit a drop in one place. It covers the whole face of it. So send in all the rays at once.
Everywhere else, the light is spread thin. But near forty-two degrees, the rays pile up into a bright beam.
Every raindrop in the sky is doing this, sending out a cone of concentrated light at forty-two degrees.
So where do the colours come from?
White sunlight is a mix of every colour, and water bends blue light slightly more than red.
That shifts the turning point. Red piles up at about forty-two and a half degrees. Violet, at about forty and a half.
Every colour in between gets its own angle.
So one drop doesn't send you a rainbow. It sends each colour off in a slightly different direction.
Now put yourself in the picture. The sun is behind you, and rain is falling in front of you.
Which drops send their red light into your eye?
Only the ones sitting forty-two degrees away from the point directly opposite the sun. That's the spot where the shadow of your head falls.
The drops keep falling, but there is always one in the right place, so the colour stays put.
Seen from where you stand, all the drops at that angle form a circle around that point. That circle is the red band.
Slightly inside it, a different set of drops sends you violet, and the other colours fall in between.
This is why you can never reach the end of a rainbow. It isn't located anywhere.
Take a step, and a different set of drops is now at forty-two degrees from you. The bow moves with you.
The person standing next to you sees a different rainbow, made by different drops.
It's also why rainbows show up in the morning and the late afternoon. As the sun climbs, the centre of the circle sinks further below the horizon.
Once the sun is higher than forty-two degrees, the whole bow is below the horizon, and there is nothing to see.
And from an aeroplane, with no ground in the way, you can see the full circle.
Sometimes there's a second, fainter bow outside the first.
That's light that bounced twice inside the drop before leaving.
Two bounces give a different turning point, about ten degrees further out, and they flip the order of the colours.
Between the two bows, the sky looks darker. No drop sends light back at those angles. It's called Alexander's band.
And inside the main bow, the sky is brighter, lit by all the light that came back at smaller angles.
So a rainbow is not an object.
It's what you get when millions of tiny spheres each fold sunlight back at the same angle, and you happen to be standing in the right place to catch it.
Next time you see one, check. The sun will be directly behind you, and the centre of the bow will be at the shadow of your own head.
That's why it does that.
